raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old woman was referred to a tertiary liver centre with a short history of nausea and right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back. A large epigastric mass could be felt on examination. Serum inflammatory markers were raised (white cell count of 19.2 x 109/l and C-reactive protein of 210mg/l); other blood tests were normal. Contrast enhanced computed tomography showed a 16cm x 16cm cystic lesion in the right lobe of the liver, exerting significant mass effect with almost complete compression of the inferior vena cava and portal vein bifurcation (Fig 1). A hydatid cyst could not be ruled out on radiology. Serology was therefore awaited prior to attempting percutaneous aspiration. 
One day after admission to our unit,the patient became profoundly confused. This was attributed initially to new hyponatraemia of unknown cause (sodium 112mmol/l) and sepsis secondary to the infected cyst. Worsening liver function with elevated enzymes and deranged clotting (alanine transaminase [ALT] 2,650iu/l and prothrombin time 35.7seconds) supported a diagnosis of acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy.
The patient developed multiorgan dysfunction requiring inotropic, ventilatory and renal support on the intensive care unit. Cardiac output studies showed a cardiac index of 1.4l/min/m2 (normal range: 2.5-4.0l/min/m2).
Bedside ultrasonography confirmed the large cystic structure with increased echogenicity. No hepatic vein flow could be identified, in keeping with hepatic outflow obstruction (secondary BCS).
The patient became increasingly unstable and hypotensive, and poor ventilation resulted in an emergency laparotomy, performed via a rooftop incision. Two litres of foul smelling, purulent material was drained from the cyst, the cyst wall was excised and the abdominal cavity was washed out thoroughly. Hydatid precautions, including scolicidal agents, were used in theatre. Liver biopsies were taken to look for underlying liver disease. Postoperatively, the patient returned to the intensive care unit for continued organ support; her cardiac index rapidly returned to normal (4.0l/min/m2). She subsequently made a slow but full recovery.
Cystic fluid aspirates taken intraoperatively later confirmed no evidence of Echinococcus on parasitology studies and cultured mixed coliforms. The fibrous cyst wall contained inflammatory cells and foci of hepatocytes with no evidence of malignancy, confirming a simple liver cyst. Liver biopsies showed severe, confluent, bridging necrosis in a predominantly centrilobular distribution, with no evidence of parenchymal liver disease (Fig 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old woman presented with a short history of nausea and right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred to a tertiary liver center with acute-onset right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back and nausea. One day after admission, she rapidly deteriorated with profound confusion, severe hyponatremia, acute liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and multiorgan dysfunction.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back, nausea, and acute confusion.

objective.physical_examination: A large epigastric mass was palpable on admission; on hospital day 2, she became profoundly encephalopathic, hypotensive, and hemodynamically unstable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed WBC 19.2 x 10^9/L and CRP 210 mg/L with normal baseline LFTs. On hospital day 2, labs showed severe hyponatremia (sodium 112 mmol/L), ALT 2,650 IU/L, and PT 35.7 seconds; cardiac output monitoring showed a depressed cardiac index of 1.4 L/min/m2 (normal 2.5-4.0 L/min/m2). Bedside Doppler ultrasound confirmed a large echogenic hepatic cyst with absent hepatic vein flow consistent with secondary Budd-Chiari syndrome.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 16 x 16 cm cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe causing near-complete compression of the inferior vena cava and portal vein bifurcation. Emergency rooftop laparotomy drained 2 liters of foul-smelling pus and excised the cyst wall under scolicidal precautions; cyst fluid parasitology was negative for Echinococcus and cultured mixed coliforms, while cyst wall and liver biopsies confirmed a secondarily infected simple hepatic cyst causing severe centrilobular bridging hepatic necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Giant simple hepatic cyst (16 x 16 cm) complicated by secondary coliform infection (pyogenic abscess) and acute inferior vena cava/hepatic vein outflow obstruction (secondary Budd-Chiari syndrome) leading to fulminant hepatic failure and septic/obstructive shock (hydatid cyst excluded by negative parasitology). Following emergency surgical drainage and cyst wall excision, her cardiac index immediately normalized to 4.0 L/min/m2 in the ICU, and she achieved a full recovery.
